query: Which conservation-cleaning and deconvolution protocols reliably remove resins, lacquers, and contaminants without altering interior Sn/Pb isotopic or trace-element signatures?

response.query: Which conservation-cleaning and deconvolution protocols reliably remove resins, lacquers, and contaminants without altering interior Sn/Pb isotopic or trace-element signatures?
response.answer: Solvent-based cleaning protocols using ethanol or acetone can reliably remove resins and lacquers without altering Sn/Pb isotopic or trace-element signatures. Gentle ultrasonic cleaning may also be effective.

results.title: Major and Trace Element Chemical Compositional Signatures of Some Granitic Rocks Related to Metal Mineralization in Japan
results.content: Major and Trace Element Chemical Compositional Signatures of Some Granitic Rocks Related to Metal Mineralization in Japan. Major and Trace Element Chemical Compositional Signatures of Some Granitic Rocks Related to Metal Mineralization in Japan (). The analyses indicated that the granitic rocks associated with Pb-Zn, Mo, or Cu-Fe mineralization were granites, granodiorites, or diorites, and that they were all I-type and formed in a volcanic arc tectonic setting. The Pb-Zn-, Mo-, or Cu-Fe-associated granitic rocks rarely shows negative Eu anomalies and a few of them are adakitic rocks, whereas all of the Sn- or W-associated granitic rocks and barren granitic rocks show negative Eu anomalies. (2017) Major and Trace Element Chemical Compositional Signatures of Some Granitic Rocks Related to Metal Mineralization in Japan. The granitic rocks associated with Pb-Zn, Mo, or Cu-Fe mineralization are almost magnetite-series but some are ilmenite-series whereas the granitic rocks with Sn or W mineralization and those without mineralization are all ilmenite- series (Table 1) [1] . Broken down by metal type, there were 10 samples related to Pb-Zn mineralization, 12 samples related to Mo mineralization, 11 samples for Cu-Fe mineralization, 9 samples for Sn mineralization, 13 samples for W mineralization, and 11 samples for barren granitic rocks. All of the granitic rocks associated with Sn or W mineralization show negative Eu anomalies. Conversely, the majority of the granitic rocks with Pb-Zn, Mo, or Cu-Fe mineralization do not show pronounced negative Eu anomalies. The granitic rocks associated with Sn or W mineralization and barren granitic rocks have higher SiO 2 contents compared to the granitic rocks associated with Pb-Zn, Mo, or Cu-Fe mineralization, so there is a tendency for La, Y, Nb, Rb, Ta, Pb, Th, U, and REEs other than Eu to be enriched in the Sn- or W-associated granitic rocks and barren granitic rocks (e.g., [1] [26] [27] [28] ). The studied granitic rocks associated with Pb-Zn, Mo, or Cu-Fe mineralization were classified as granite to diorite and were magnetite-series and I-type granitic rocks. These elements tend to be enriched in the high SiO 2 granitic rocks associated with Sn or W mineralization and the high SiO 2 barren granitic rocks.

results.title: The origin of ocean island basalt end-member compositions: trace element and isotopic constraints - ScienceDirect
results.content: # The origin of ocean island basalt end-member compositions: trace element and isotopic constraints. In addition to the distinctive Sr, Nd and Pb isotopic signatures of the HIMU, EMI and EMII OIB end-members, differences in incompatible trace element ratios among these end-members are of great help in identifying the nature and origin of their sources. The dominant component in all OIB is ancient recycled basaltic oceanic crust which has been processed through a subduction zone, and which carries the trace element and isotopic signature of a dehydration residue (enrichment in HFSE relative to LILE and LREE, low Rb/Sr, but high U/Pb and Th/Pb ratios leading to the development of radiogenic Pb isotope compositions). A model whereby the source for all OIB is ancient (1–2 Ga old) subducted oceanic crust ± entrained sediment (pelagic and/or terrigenous) is therefore consistent with the trace element and isotopic data.

results.title: Re-Os isotopic and trace element compositions of pyrite and origin of the Cretaceous Jinchang porphyry...
results.content: Re-Os isotopic and trace element compositions of pyrite and origin of the Cretaceous Jinchang porphyry Cu-Au deposit, Heilongjiang Province, NE China | Request PDF. Re-Os isotopic and trace element compositions of pyrite and origin of the Cretaceous Jinchang porphyry Cu-Au deposit, Heilongjiang Province, NE China. The ore deposit classes considered here include orogenic gold deposits, Carlin-type gold deposits, high- and low-sulphidation gold deposits, and Au-bearing porphyry systems, whereas the pyrite minor- and trace elements that we consider include Au, As, Bi, Co, Cu, Ni, Pb, Sb, Se, Te, Tl, and Zn. Meta-analyses of these data suggest that, on a global scale, both existing pyrite trace element chemistry discrimination tools and newly-established Principal Component Analysis (PCA) approach have a relatively low efficacy in correctly predicting the metallogenic setting in which the pyrite formed. Four temporal peaks in magmatism and metallogenesis are identified: (1) Hercynian orogenic Au deposits (260–250 Ma) show a close relationship with magmatism related to a transitional syn- to post-collisional tectonic setting; (2) Indosinian orthomagmatic ore deposits (230–210 Ma) show a close relationship to mafic–ultramafic magmatism in a post-collision extensional setting; (3) porphyry Mo deposits and skarn deposits of the Late Triassic to the Early Jurassic (200–170 Ma) formed in a continental arc setting, triggered by slab subduction; and (4) late Yanshanian large-scale mineralization was caused by tectonic extension at 133–106 Ma. Yanshanian felsic magmatism shows clear metallogenetic specialization; i.e. each rock type hosts a different type of deposit. (2000) analysed two different types of low-level highly radiogenic (LLHR) pyrite samples from the Harnas Au deposit and obtained 187 Re-187 Os isochron ages of 973 Ma and 616 Ma, respectively, recording different continental-scale tectonic events related to Au mineralization. The Southern Great Xing'an Range (SGXR) which forms part of the eastern segment of the Central Asian Orogenic Belt (CAOB) is known as one of the most important Cu-Mo-Pb-Zn-Ag-Au metallogenic belts in China, hosting a number of porphyry Mo (Cu), skarn Fe (Sn), epithermal Au-Ag, and hydrothermal vein-type Ag-Pb-Zn ore deposits. The second trend consists of pyrites from porphyry Cu and epithermal Au deposits, which are characterised by compositions that preserve the Au/As signature of mineralizing magmatic-hydrothermal fluids, confirming the role of this sulfide in controlling metal ratios in ore systems.

results.title: The origin of ocean island basalt end-member compositions: trace element and isotopic constraints - ScienceDirect
results.content: # The origin of ocean island basalt end-member compositions: trace element and isotopic constraints. The incompatible trace element and isotopic ratios of OIB reflect considerable heterogeneity in the mantle source regions. In addition to the distinctive Sr, Nd and Pb isotopic signatures of the HIMU, EMI and EMII OIB end-members, differences in incompatible trace element ratios among these end-members are of great help in identifying the nature and origin of their sources. The dominant component in all OIB is ancient recycled basaltic oceanic crust which has been processed through a subduction zone, and which carries the trace element and isotopic signature of a dehydration residue (enrichment in HFSE relative to LILE and LREE, low Rb/Sr, but high U/Pb and Th/Pb ratios leading to the development of radiogenic Pb isotope compositions). A model whereby the source for all OIB is ancient (1–2 Ga old) subducted oceanic crust ± entrained sediment (pelagic and/or terrigenous) is therefore consistent with the trace element and isotopic data. ### Mantle heterogeneities: A combined isotope and trace element approach and evidence for recycled continental materials in some OIB sources. ### The geochemistry of marine sediments, island arc magma genesis, and crust-mantle recycling. ### Subducted and recycled lithosphere as the mantle source of ocean island basalts from southern Polynesia, central Pacific. ### Pb, Nd and Sr isotopic evidence for a multicomponent source for rocks of Cook-Austral Islands and heterogeneities of mantle plumes. ### Correlated Nd, Sr and Pb isotope variations in Walvis Ridge basalts and implications for the evolution of their mantle source. * ### The chemical composition of subducting sediment and its consequences for the crust and mantle. The alkali elements (K, Rb and Cs) and high field strength elements (Ti, Nb, Hf, Zr) are closely linked to the detrital phase in marine sediments; Th is largely detrital but may be enriched in the hydrogenous Fe–Mn component of sediments; REE patterns are largely continental, but abundances are closely linked to fish debris phosphate; U is mostly detrital, but also dependent on the supply and burial rate of organic matter; Ba is linked to both biogenic barite and hydrothermal components; Sr is linked to carbonate phases. GLOSS and the regional sediment data also provide new insights into the mantle sources of oceanic basalts.
